story.headline: Drinking 2–3 cups of coffee a day linked to dramatically lower dementia risk
story.summary: Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee daily was linked to a dramatically lower risk of dementia and better cognitive functioning in a study spanning up to 43 years. The benefits appeared regardless of genetic risk, but decaffeinated coffee did not show the same association.
story.score_reason: Coffee & dementia credible, universal but no local

carousel.cover_headline:
2–3 Cups of Coffee a Day
Linked to Much Lower
Dementia Risk

slides.label: THE STUDY
slides.headline: U.S. adults tracked for up to 43 years
slides.insight: Researchers linked daily caffeinated coffee to lower dementia rates over decades.

slides.label: THE NUMBER
slides.headline: **141** vs 330 dementia cases per 100,000 people yearly
slides.insight: Higher coffee drinkers showed far fewer dementia cases than those who rarely drank it.

slides.label: COGNITIVE HEALTH
slides.headline: 7.8% vs 9.5% reported memory or thinking decline
slides.insight: Adults drinking more caffeinated coffee were less likely to notice cognitive decline themselves.

slides.label: WHAT TO KNOW
slides.headline: Decaf showed no same link — caffeine may matter
slides.insight: Tea was also linked to better cognitive outcomes. This is association, not proven cause.
slides.image_prompt: tea and coffee side by side

slides.label: TRY THIS WEEK
slides.headline: Swap one sugary drink for plain caffeinated coffee or tea
slides.insight: No added sugar. See how your morning focus feels after a few days.

sources: Study of U.S. adults, 2026 (reported by ScienceDaily Nutrition)
carousel.caption:
2–3 cups of caffeinated coffee a day was linked to much lower dementia risk in a long-running U.S. study.

Researchers tracked adults for up to 43 years and found 141 dementia cases per 100,000 yearly among higher coffee drinkers, versus 330 among those who rarely drank it. Decaf did not show the same link. Tea was also associated with better cognitive outcomes. This is an association study — other lifestyle factors may also play a role. Could your daily kopi be doing more than you thought?

Not medical advice.

Sources: Study of U.S. adults, 2026 (ScienceDaily Nutrition)
